data.content_ref: inline:The target is internally inconsistent: it claims to 'bypass induction by shifting the framework from justification to selection,' yet the very thing it purports to defend is a normative *preference* for the best-corroborated theory, which is forward-looking and action-guiding. Biological selection is purely retrospective — it explains why the current population composition is what it is, not what one *should* choose going forward. To convert the descriptive fact 'theory T survived tests S1…Sn' into the normative 'we should prefer T' requires exactly the inductive bridge (past performance licenses future expectation) the target disavows. The mechanism's own gloss — 'we prefer... because it is the only one currently known to be adapted to the problem environment' — is either (a) a purely present-tense description, in which case it has no normative force and the word 'defensible' is unwarranted, or (b) a tacit inductive inference from adaptation to suitability-for-use, in which case the claim does not bypass induction and contradicts its central assertion. The countercondition 'If robustness is merely a synonym for high probability' gestures at this tension but does not resolve it; the target needs an independent, non-inductive account of why 'robustness against error elimination' ought to guide preference, and none is supplied. Thus the claim smuggles in the very justification it promises to eliminate.
